summary:
Costa Rica decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1971 and adopted marriage equality in 2020, the first Central American country to do so. Outright International (updated 12 March 2026) and the ILGA World Database both record the resulting LGBTI legal framework, covering same-sex conduct, gender recognition and legal protections.

Legal gender recognition is administrative rather than judicial. Executive Decree 41173-MP, in force since 2018, permits a change of gender marker on identity documents without surgery and without a court order. Since May 2018 name changes on official identification have been available through a simple, free procedure at the Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones; before that, from 2013, transgender people could change their legal name only on a judicial order. A 2016 bill that would have allowed transgender people to change both name and gender without surgery or judicial permission did not pass.

The state health system funds gender-affirming care. The UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, reporting on her July 2023 visit (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024), praised near-universal coverage and identified good practices in specific legislation while raising concern about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups, and recommending intersectional data collection.

The Legislative Assembly strengthened hate-crime penalties in 2020. Amendments to the Penal Code provide 20 to 35 years' imprisonment for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation (article 112), one to three years for exclusion or segregation on that basis (article 380), and three to ten years for inflicting physical or mental pain, intimidation, coercion or blackmail on that basis (article 386bis). The inventory does not state that gender identity is a listed motivating ground in these provisions.

No current visa or entry rule targets LGBTQ travellers. In December 2018 the President signed executive decrees covering immigration rights for binational same-sex couples. A 1990 instruction from the Minister of the Interior directing consulates to refuse visas to women travelling without a man, intended to block foreign lesbians from attending an international meeting, is decades old and is not described as current policy.

Prison placement for transgender detainees is governed by a stated policy that has not produced consistent results. In June 2017 the Justice Ministry, through Vice-Minister Marco Feoli, announced that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual may choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility, with relocation strictly voluntary, decided case by case with prison social workers and psychologists; a circular ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners and an exclusive module for trans people was under consideration, with Spain's system cited as the model and vulnerable-population protocols developed with a regional human-rights organisation since 2016. By June 2019 a trans woman was held at CAI Orosi de Cartago, a men's facility, having transitioned while incarcerated, and the Justice Ministry confirmed 23 transgender people in the national prison system at the time. She recounted identity-targeted abuse including a rape with a broomstick-handle at La Reforma in Alajuela, witnessed by a custodian.

Rollback pressure is documented alongside these protections. A conversion-therapy bill has stalled since its 2019 committee report, and in 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education program and the 2022 anti-LGBT-bullying protocol.
tangentialFactors:
Official recognition of LGBTI dates sits beside organised political resistance. The government officially recognised the International Day Against Homophobia on 17 May in 2008, when President Óscar Arias and Health Minister María Luisa Avila directed public institutions to facilitate and support activities directed at the eradication of homophobia; in 2014 President Luis Guillermo Solís flew the rainbow flag at the Casa Presidencial on an equal mast with the national flag, prompting lawmakers from PASE, National Restoration and other conservative parties to call it a provocation while a same-sex civil union bill was pending. President Carlos Alvarado Quesada became the first Costa Rican President to march at the annual pride parade in San José in June 2019, an event drawing about 100,000 participants.

In 2018 President Alvarado issued a public apology to the LGBT community for past state persecution, citing state-promoted and executed persecutions, raids, arbitrary arrests and beatings. Police harassment and raids of LGBTQ people and private establishments were formerly commonplace while homosexuality was technically legal.

Sexual orientation and gender identity questions have been sustained political flashpoints. The 2018 general election was sharply divisive over same-sex marriage, and a 2012 poll found 60% of 18-to-34-year-olds supported equal rights for same-sex couples. The Supreme Court ruled in 2000 that a gay sauna must remain open, holding that subjective criteria of morality and proper behaviour have no legal basis, and in 2011 reversed its 2008 ruling to allow same-sex couples equal access to conjugal visits in prison; the same court found in 2000 that IVF is unconstitutional. Survivor's pensions were extended to same-sex partners under all national-budget pension plans by a Ministry of Labor announcement of 25 June 2016, with an individual survivor benefit approved on 29 June 2018, while the teachers' separate budget was excluded.
localsOnly:
Transgender residents change their gender marker through an administrative route under Executive Decree 41173-MP with no surgery and no court order, and change their name on official identification at the Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones through a free procedure, in place since May 2018. The state health system funds gender-affirming care.

Resident-facing services have narrowed in the last two years. Authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education program in 2025 and withdrew the 2022 anti-LGBT-bullying protocol; a conversion-therapy bill has sat without movement since its 2019 committee report. Comprehensive sex education in public high schools is described as almost nonexistent because of opposition from the Catholic Church and other religious groups.

The Justice Ministry's 2017 circular ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners and left an exclusive module for trans people under consideration, and protocols for vulnerable prison populations were developed with a regional human-rights organisation from 2016. The voluntary placement choice announced in 2017 remains the stated policy; the 2019 reporting shows it operating case by case rather than systematically.

Institutional discrimination has been challenged domestically. In 1993 the Universidad Internacional de las Américas was found to have a policy of expelling LGBTQ students and firing LGBTQ faculty and staff; the Ministry of Education responded that enforcing it would likely violate constitutional articles 20, 33 and 70.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether gender identity, as distinct from sexual orientation, is a statutory aggravating ground in the 2020 Penal Code amendments is not resolved by the inventory; every penalty listed is framed around sexual orientation.

The current operational status of the 2017 prison placement policy after 2019 is not sourced. The inventory does not establish whether the census and the proposed trans-only module were completed, or how many of the 23 transgender prisoners recorded in 2019 were held in facilities matching their gender identity.

The inventory does not say whether the December 2018 decrees on immigration rights for binational same-sex couples have been amended, narrowed or challenged since entry into force, nor whether the definition of binational couple covers unmarried partners.

The UN Special Rapporteur's recommendations on intersectional data collection and on a moratorium on applying criminal laws in certain health contexts are recorded as recommendations; their implementation is not sourced.

The extension of survivor's pension rights to same-sex partners is documented through 2016 and 2018 announcements; whether trans spouses and partners are covered under the same plans, and whether the teachers' budget exclusion was later closed, is unresolved.
